cards.when: a cross-section of non-negative values (incomes/wealth/shares) → a scalar inequality index or the Lorenz curve as numeric data; descriptive/distributional at one point in time
cards.when_not: a return tail (VaR/ES→#65); a conditional-on-X tail/GaR (→#64); poverty/concentration indices (pov/conc are not exposed); a within/between Theil decomposition by group; time-series dynamics

alternatives.criterion: a headline single number, the most comparable; sensitive mainly to the centre of the distribution
you want an additive within/between decomposition (the GE family); entropy@1==Theil@0==Theil's T/GE(1) (upper tail), entropy@0==Theil@1==mean log deviation/GE(0) (lower tail)
you want an explicit inequality-aversion parameter epsilon (normative/welfare)
you want absolute inequality (invariant to adding a constant), not relative
Ricci-Schutz/Pietra: the share of the total that would have to be redistributed (Robin Hood)
a non-parametric comparison: if curve A lies everywhere above B ⇒ unambiguously less inequality (stronger than a scalar)

alternatives.alt: category 12 (#64 quantile regression / #65 VaR and Expected Shortfall)
alternatives.criterion: a conditional-on-X tail (GaR) or return risk metrics — a different question

output_key_fields: index (compute_inequality): the scalar index; Gini/Atkinson/RS ∈ [0,1] (0 = equality), Theil/entropy >= 0 (NOT a percentage), Kolm in units of x (absolute), var = CV and square_var = CV²
type (compute_inequality): which index was computed (a closed enum, default Gini)
parameter (compute_inequality): blank ⇒ the index default (Atkinson 0.5, Kolm 1, entropy 0.5, Theil 0), NOT 'no parameter'
n (compute_inequality): the sample size
p (lorenz_curve): the cumulative population share (a chart-ready array)
L (lorenz_curve): the ordinary Lorenz curve — the bottom p*100% holds L(p)*100% of the total; relative inequality
L_general (lorenz_curve): the generalized Lorenz curve = L × mean (units of x); it embeds the level → a welfare comparison
gini (lorenz_curve): the Gini of the same series, for consistency; n: the size
interpretation_traps: Theil/entropy are NOT bounded at 1 — do not read them as a percentage; only Gini/Atkinson/RS∈[0,1]
Kolm is absolute (units of x), not a 0-1 relative index — do not compare it with the Gini

in ineq the parameter is inverted between the two types: entropy@1==Theil@0 (==the Theil default; Theil's T/GE(1), upper tail), entropy@0==Theil@1 (mean log deviation/GE(0), lower tail): the same number, a different name/tail
a blank parameter in the output ⇒ the index default, NOT 'no parameter'
non-negativity is enforced ONLY for Gini/Atkinson/Theil/entropy and the Lorenz curve; RS/Kolm/var/square_var accept negatives, and the underlying index routine does not error on them
all zeros: it passes the >=0 gate but Lc divides by 0 → NaN→JSON null; the wrapper blocks it with a sum(x)>0 gate
ordinary L (shape) vs generalized L_general (shape+level): the same L does not mean the same welfare if the mean differs (Shorrocks)
sources: Cowell 2000 Measurement of Inequality (Handbook of Income Distribution)
Atkinson 1970 JET 2:244 (Atkinson index & inequality aversion)
Theil 1967 Economics and Information Theory (Theil/entropy indices)
Arnold 1987 Majorization and the Lorenz Order, Springer (Lorenz dominance)
Shorrocks 1983 Economica 50:3 (generalized Lorenz)
Kolm 1976 JET 12:416 (absolute inequality)

cards.method: tax progressivity & redistribution + subgroup decomposition of inequality (extended/S-Gini · concentration · Atkinson · GEI · Lorenz)
cards.when: a cross-section of non-negative values (income/wealth/tax/expenditure) when you want (a) a single-parameter/extended Gini with an explicit tail weight (param), an Atkinson index (aversion epsilon), a GEI (Theil/MLD), (b) a concentration index ranked by ANOTHER variable → the building blocks of Kakwani progressivity/Reynolds-Smolensky redistribution, (c) the Lorenz curve as numeric data, or (d) a SUBGROUP decomposition into within/between/(overlap|stratif|cross|residual) by a factor
cards.when_not: a plain scalar index with no tail parameter/decomposition → #91 ineq (Gini/RS/Kolm/var); a return tail VaR/ES → #65; a conditional-on-X GaR → #64; poverty indices (FGT) — not exposed; time-series dynamics

alternatives.criterion: a headline scalar Gini/Theil/Atkinson/Kolm WITHOUT a group decomposition and WITHOUT an extended-Gini param — a simpler surface
an extended Gini with an explicit weight on the poor (param=2 is the classic Gini; a larger param → more sensitivity to the lower tail)
you want a FULLY ADDITIVE within+between decomposition (the GE family)
BDA is multiplicative (1-(1-w)(1-b)) with a cross term; DP is additive (within+between+residual) — choose according to your reference framework
Kakwani progressivity = C_tax - G_preTax; Reynolds-Smolensky = G_preTax - C_postTax — the redistributive analysis of taxes/benefits
a non-parametric comparison of distributions (curve A everywhere above B ⇒ unambiguously less inequality)

output_key_fields: index (ineqd_sgini / ineqd_sconc / ineqd_atkinson / ineqd_gei): the scalar index; index_name (SGini/SConc/Atk/GEI); parameter and parameter_name (param/epsilon/alpha); n; weighted
p (ineqd_lorenz): the cumulative population share (n+1 points, chart-ready); L: the ordinary Lorenz curve; L_general: the generalized one, L times the mean, in units of x; plus gini and mean

within/between (the ineqd_decomp_* nodes): the within- and between-group inequality; third_component and third_name (overlap, stratification, cross or residual); between_elmo, the Elbers 'maximum' between-group term (blank when it is not requested, and OUTSIDE the identity)

reconciled_total and reconcile_error (the ineqd_decomp_* nodes): the recomposition check, |total - sum(components)| <= 1e-6; plus decomp_method; groups, a frame per group with group/index/share/weight and optionally contribution; and n_groups
interpretation_traps: the EXTENDED GINI param: param=2 == the classic Gini; param>1 weights the poor; param->1 => 0; 0<param<1 => a NEGATIVE index (a mathematically valid S-Gini, NOT conventional inequality — for a headline figure use param>=1)

the ATKINSON DECOMPOSITION: BDA is MULTIPLICATIVE (total=1-(1-within)(1-between)) — do NOT add within+between+cross (it does not equal the total; the 'cross' term = within+between-total); DP is ADDITIVE (within+between+residual)
the GEI is FULLY ADDITIVE (total=within+between); the SGini BM decomposition is within+between+overlap, YL is within+between+stratif; betweenELMO is NOT part of any identity

KAKWANI/REDISTRIBUTION = the DIFFERENCE between a concentration index and a Gini, NOT a single output: Kakwani progressivity = C_tax - G_preTax (positive=progressive); Reynolds-Smolensky = G_preTax - C_postTax; the wrapper supplies the building blocks, the difference is taken downstream
STRICT POSITIVITY: Atkinson with epsilon==1, and the GEI with alpha in {0,1}, require x>0 — a zero makes the raw routine return nothing at all; other values of epsilon or alpha accept zeros

SILENTLY WRONG (gated by the wrapper): a negative x returns nothing; a gap in x or w is silently removed; a wrong weight length is silently recycled; a non-categorical grouping variable returns nothing; an extreme alpha overflows to infinity
GEI alpha: alpha=1 is Theil-T/GE(1) (the upper tail); alpha=0 is the mean log deviation/GE(0) (the lower tail); alpha=2 is half the CV²
sources: Kakwani N.C. (1977) Measurement of Tax Progressivity, Economic Journal 87(345):71-80 (concentration/progressivity)
Atkinson A.B. (1970) On the Measurement of Inequality, JET 2:244-263
Blackorby C., Donaldson D., Auersperg M. (1981) Canadian J. Economics 14:665-685 (the BDA Atkinson decomposition)
Das T., Parikh A. (1982) Empirical Economics 7:23-48 (the DP Atkinson decomposition)
Bhattacharya N., Mahalanobis B. (1967) JASA 62:143-161 (the BM Gini decomposition); Yitzhaki S., Lerman R. (1991) Review of Income and Wealth 37:313 (YL stratification)
Shorrocks A.F. (1980) The Class of Additively Decomposable Inequality Measures, Econometrica 48:613-625 (GE within/between); Elbers et al. (2005) World Bank WP 3687 (the ELMO maximum between)
Reynolds M., Smolensky E. (1977) Public Expenditure, Taxes and the Distribution of Income (the redistribution effect)

cards.method: drivers of inequality change: RIF (recentered influence function) regressions + regression-based (Fields/Yun) inequality decomposition
cards.when: you want to explain WHAT DRIVES inequality (not merely to measure it): (a) the marginal effect of covariates on a distributional statistic (quantile/gini/variance) through a RIF regression; (b) a decomposition of the Gini/MLD into within/between/overlap by subgroup; (c) a Fields regression-based decomposition of total inequality across several characteristics; (d) a Yun decomposition of the CHANGE in inequality between two years into a price vs a quantity effect. Income micro data with survey weights + covariates
cards.when_not: a plain scalar index or Lorenz curve with no covariates (-> #91); tax progressivity or a single-index decomposition (-> #224); a parametric income distribution (-> #227); a conditional outcome tail or Growth-at-Risk (-> #64); return risk metrics, VaR and ES (-> #65); time-series dynamics

alternatives.criterion: you want the influence of each observation on the index itself (an input for a downstream RIF regression or a health-inequality decomposition); recentering: the weighted mean == the index

alternatives.alt: rif_regression (a deterministic OLS on the RIF)
alternatives.criterion: the marginal effects of covariates on a quantile/gini/variance, fast, without inference; it supports a vector of quantiles (unconditional quantile regression, Firpo-Fortin-Lemieux)
you need statistical inference on the RIF coefficients; ONE quantile only; SEEDED (deterministic)
you want the within/between + overlap (interaction) term of the Gini by one categorical variable; the Gini does NOT decompose cleanly (the overlap != 0 when the group distributions overlap)
you want a CLEAN within+between decomposition (no overlap) by one categorical variable; the mean log deviation = the generalized entropy GE(0), additively decomposable
SEVERAL characteristics at once: the contribution of each covariate (+ the residual) to total inequality (4 indices: gini/mld/theil/var-log); they sum to 100%

you compare two years/datasets: a decomposition of the CHANGE in the variance of log income by characteristic into a price effect (a change in the coefficients) vs a quantity effect (a change in composition)

output_key_fields: rif (rif_influence): the numeric RIF vector (chart-ready); recentered_stat: the index — the weighted mean of the RIF equals the index, verified live; method/quantile/kernel/weighted/n

coefficients (rif_regression): a SINGLE frame (term, quantile, coef, se, t, p) — normalised per quantile, since the raw routine changes shape with the method; adjusted_r2 and df; plus the raw fit as a stub
coefficients (rif_regression_se): a frame (term, coef, lower, upper, se, z_value, p_value, signif); Nboot/confidence/seed echoed; deterministic given the seed

decomposition (gini_decomposition): a named record (gini_total, gini_within, gini_between, gini_overlap — they do NOT add up without the overlap); a by_group frame (gini/contribution/mean/share_pop/share_income/n); gini_group_contribution sums to gini_within

decomposition (mld_decomposition): a named record (mld_total, mld_within, mld_between — within plus between equals the total, with NO overlap); a by_group frame; n_deleted, the non-positive values the logarithm drops; plus a note

inequality_measures (ineq_regression_decomp): a named record (gini, mld, theil, variance_logincome); a decomposition frame (variable, contribution — summing to 1); adjusted_r2/r_squared; n_deleted/n_used; plus a note

variance_logincome (ineq_change_decomp): (year1, year2, change); the change_absolute and change_relative frames (variable, price, quantity, total); residual_absolute/residual_relative; the Yun identity holds: the sum of price and quantity, plus the residual, equals the change
interpretation_traps: a DUAL weights convention: rif/gini_decomp/mld_decomp take weights = a numeric VECTOR; rifr/rifrSE/dineq_rb/dineq_change_rb take weights = a COLUMN NAME (a string) inside data — the wrong type = a silent error/misalignment

rifr CHANGES ITS OUTPUT SHAPE per method (quantile: Coef/SE/t/p matrices; gini/variance: a coefficients matrix + a scalar r2) — the wrapper normalises it into ONE long-format data_frame; do not rely on the raw shape
rifrSE accepts a scalar quantile ONLY (a vector → 'condition has length > 1'); it is a BOOTSTRAP → SEEDED (the same seed = identical results)
the log-based methods (mld/dineq_rb/dineq_change_rb) SILENTLY DROP x<=0 → always read n_deleted/note; if you miss it you overstate n
the Gini overlap term != 0 when the group distributions overlap → within+between do NOT sum to the total (unlike the MLD, which is purely additive); do not ignore the overlap

silently wrong: the raw routine drops incomplete cases in x and z, sets a missing weight to 0, and recycles when the weight or group vector is the wrong length; a zero weight then blanks the RIF silently — the wrapper enforces no gaps, a length equal to n, and weights STRICTLY above 0

gini_decomp does NOT filter negative x → a silently wrong Gini; the wrapper enforces an x>=0 gate (project-side); kernel='rectangular' with a gap around the quantile → dq=0 → Inf (the finite post-gate blocks it)

the formula nodes (rif_regression, rif_regression_se, ineq_regression_decomp, ineq_change_decomp): a gap in ANY covariate is blocked by a gate, because the underlying fit would silently drop those rows while reporting '0 deleted' and an inflated n_used; complete cases are required in every variable of the formula
sources: Firpo, Fortin & Lemieux 2009 (Econometrica 77:953, Unconditional Quantile Regressions — the RIF)
Fields 2003 (Research in Labor Economics 22:1, regression-based inequality decomposition)
Yun 2006 / Brewer & Wren-Lewis 2016 (Oxford Bull. Econ. Stat. 78:289, accounting for changes in income inequality — price vs quantity)
Mookherjee & Shorrocks 1982 (Economic Journal 92:886, the MLD within/between decomposition)
Heckley, Gerdtham & Kjellsson 2016 (J. Health Economics 48:89, a general RIF decomposition of socioeconomic inequality)

cards.method: Complex-survey-aware inequality & poverty with design-based linearized SE (Gini/QSR/Zenga + FGT/ARPR)
cards.when: you have survey MICRODATA (a microdata data_frame) with sampling weights/strata/clusters and you want an inequality index (gini/qsr/zenga) or a poverty index (FGT/ARPR) WITH a correct design-based (linearized) standard error + CI + degrees of freedom; the node builds the survey design and the linearisation internally
cards.when_not: a plain vector with no complex-survey design -> #91 (a scalar index or Lorenz curve, with no standard errors); replicate-weight designs — not exposed; a return tail VaR or ES -> #65; a conditional Growth-at-Risk -> #64; the other design-based inequality estimators (GEI, Atkinson, Rényi, Watts, the median poverty gap) — future candidates

alternatives.criterion: a headline single-number inequality index with a design-based SE; sensitive mainly to the centre
the Quintile Share Ratio S80/S20 (alpha1=0.2, alpha2=0.8): the ratio of the upper to the lower quantile share; a Eurostat headline indicator
the Zenga (2007) uniformity index ∈[0,1]; sensitive to the whole distribution (a point-by-point comparison of lower/upper means)
Foster-Greer-Thorbecke: g=0 the headcount ratio, g=1 the poverty gap, g=2 the severity (the squared gap); an absolute (abs_thresh) or relative (relq/relm) threshold
the At-Risk-Of-Poverty Rate: the share below a relative threshold (the default is 60% of the median); a Eurostat headline poverty indicator
domain estimation (e.g. by region/group) with correctly reduced degrees of freedom
a plain vector with no survey design/weights — a descriptive index without SE

output_key_fields: estimate: the scalar index (Gini/QSR/Zenga/FGT/ARPR); Gini/Zenga/ARPR/FGT∈[0,1], QSR>=1 (a ratio)
se: the design-based LINEARIZED standard error (a Deville influence function; NOT a naive/iid SE)
ci_lower/ci_upper: a t-based CI at the given level, with the design degrees of freedom (df)
df: degf(design) — the degrees of freedom of the design (they drop in a domain subset)

measure/income: which index, and which variable; n_total/n_used/n_na: the sizes; n_used counts the observations that ACTUALLY enter the estimator (n_total minus n_na, or the count within the domain) and is NOT inflated by the incomes the estimator drops
g/type_thresh/abs_thresh (svy_poverty): the FGT parameters; alpha1/alpha2 (svy_inequality): the QSR quantiles
interpretation_traps: the linearisation step is MANDATORY: svyfgt/svyarpr/svyqsr error without it, BUT svygini/svyzenga compute SILENTLY (with a possibly wrong SE) — the wrapper always runs it
wrong ids/weights/strata → a wrong linearized SE (the estimate may be right while the SE is not); the design must reflect the ACTUAL sampling
a missing income with na_rm=False blanks the coefficient SILENTLY; the wrapper blocks that with a hard gate — set na_rm=True explicitly
the survey-design constructor SILENTLY accepts negative/zero weights; the wrapper requires weights>0
the FGT estimator with a relative threshold SILENTLY ignores abs_thresh — the wrapper requires abs_thresh to be unset unless type_thresh='abs'
FGT monotonicity: severity(g=2) <= gap(g=1) <= headcount(g=0); they differ in their sensitivity to the depth of poverty
ids="1" means ~1 (no clustering); df≈n-1; for a clustered design supply the actual PSU column
sources: Foster, Greer & Thorbecke 1984 Econometrica 52:761 (the FGT poverty measures)
Osier 2009 Survey Methodology 35:193 (the linearization of inequality/poverty estimators)
Deville 1999 Survey Methodology 25:193 (influence-function variance estimation)
Zenga 2007 Statistica & Applicazioni 5:3 (the Zenga uniformity index)
Eurostat EU-SILC methodology (ARPR at 60% of the median, the S80/S20 quintile share ratio)

cards.method: GB2 (Generalized Beta of the 2nd kind, 4 parameters a,b,p,q) parametric income-distribution ML fit + analytic Gini/ARPR
cards.when: you have microdata of POSITIVE income (optionally with survey weights) and you want a PARAMETRIC model of the whole distribution: the GB2(a,b,p,q) is fitted by ML (full + profile log-likelihood) and yields CLOSED-FORM analytic indicators (Gini, ARPR, RMPG, QSR) that smooth out sampling noise and allow comparison/simulation; or you already have estimated (a,p,q) and want an analytic Gini/ARPR
cards.when_not: a non-parametric scalar index or a Lorenz curve straight from the sample (→#91 ineq, with no distributional assumption); a RETURN tail VaR/ES (→#65) or a conditional-on-X GaR (→#64); income with zeros/negatives (the GB2 is defined on x>0 — it is rejected); a small sample where the 4-parameter ML does not converge (heavy-tail identifiability); a within/between decomposition by group

alternatives.criterion: you do not want a distributional assumption; a descriptive index straight from the sample at one point in time; the GB2 is preferable when you want smoothing, tail extrapolation, or analytic poverty/welfare metrics from a single model
the most general 4-parameter form; it needs a reasonably large sample for the full ML to converge (the convergence gate blocks it otherwise)
you already have (a,p,q) [+prop] from another source/fit and you want only the scale-free index without refitting
you explicitly want the non-converged result for diagnosis (it comes back with converged=False); NEVER as a production output — a non-converged four-parameter fit is silently wrong

alternatives.alt: category 12 (#64 quantile regression / #65 VaR and Expected Shortfall)
alternatives.criterion: a conditional-on-X tail (GaR) or return risk metrics — a different question from an income distribution

output_key_fields: a, b, p and q (fit_gb2), and params as a named vector: the four estimated GB2 parameters from the FULL ML; a is the tail shape, b the scale, and p and q the Beta-2 shapes; at convergence all are above 0

loglik and loglik_profile (fit_gb2): the CONVENTIONAL TOTAL log-likelihood — the sum of the weighted GB2 log-densities, negative and of order n — directly usable for AIC = -2*loglik + 2k, for BIC, or for a likelihood ratio; it is NOT the raw negated per-observation mean the optimiser reports
converged (fit_gb2): True only when the FULL ML optimisation returns code 0 (a FUNCTIONAL GATE); convergence_full and convergence_profile carry the raw codes (0 = ok, 1 = the iteration limit)
gini (fit_gb2): the analytic Gini(a,p,q) in [0,1] at the fitted parameters; gini_defined=False marks a heavy tail (a*q<=1) where it is undefined, so the value is blank
arpr (fit_gb2): the At-Risk-of-Poverty Rate at prop times the median (default 0.6); arpr_prop is the proportion; arpr_defined is the finiteness flag
n (fit_gb2): the sample size; indicators: a frame comparing the empirical estimate against the full and profile ML (median, mean, ARPR, RMPG, QSR, GINI, a, b, p, q) — a chart-ready comparison
gini (gini_gb2): the analytic Gini of the GB2, scale-free and depending only on a, p and q
arpr (arpr_gb2): the analytic ARPR (scale-free); prop is the poverty line as a proportion of the median
interpretation_traps: CONVERGENCE: a small or heavy-tailed sample stops the FULL ML from converging, and yet it returns parameters as if it had succeeded — the convergence gate blocks that, and converged=False is not a valid output

POSITIVE SUPPORT: zero, negative or missing incomes do NOT raise an error in the ML fit; it proceeds silently. The x>0 and no-gaps gate is imposed by the project, and the reference example itself filters to positive incomes
WEIGHTS: a wrong length of w is recycled silently, zero weights exclude observations — a gate on length==n & w>0

HEAVY-TAIL Gini: with a*q<=1 the Gini is undefined, because the expectation does not exist; the standalone gini_gb2 errors explicitly, while inside fit_gb2 the value is left blank with gini_defined=False — and the fit itself remains valid
prop: the ARPR is monotone in prop; a prop outside (0,1) silently gives a wrong value — a gate on (0,1); it is scale-free (b is irrelevant)
the gini_gb2/arpr_gb2 argument order: (shape1=a, shape2=p, shape3=q); swapping p and q changes the result — do not confuse them

cards.method: affluence/richness indices (the top-tail mirror of poverty indices): the richness headcount ratio, the Chakravarty concave T1 index, the FGT convex T2 index, the Medeiros average affluence gap, the top income share, the Medeiros affluence line — weighted implementations
cards.when: a cross-section of positive incomes (with or without population weights) → how much and how intensely wealth is concentrated in the UPPER tail: the headcount of the rich (a line at k×median), the intensity of affluence (the concave T1 / convex T2 index), the absolute mean affluence gap, the income share of the top (1-p), or constructing a Medeiros affluence line from a poverty line
cards.when_not: the inequality of the WHOLE distribution (Gini, Theil, Atkinson, Lorenz -> #91); POVERTY indices or the lower tail (the FGT family); a return tail VaR or ES (-> #65); a conditional Growth-at-Risk (-> #64); Wolfson polarization, the Palma ratio or the weighted Gini (not exposed — the Gini is covered by #91); bootstrap standard errors (stochastic, not exposed); a subgroup decomposition (not exposed)

alternatives.criterion: how many people are rich — the weighted share of the population above the affluence line (the headcount); it does not capture intensity/distance
an affluence intensity that INCREASES under a rank-preserving progressive transfer among the rich (axiom T1); bounded in [0,1]; the parameter beta>0
an affluence intensity that DECREASES under a progressive transfer among the rich (axiom T2); the parameter alpha>1; it is NOT bounded by 1
the ABSOLUTE mean affluence gap (in income units), not a ratio — the size of the excess income above the line
the share of total income of the richest (1-p) fraction — the most widely used metric (top 1%/10% shares); the threshold is the p-quantile, NOT k×median
you want the affluence LINE (not an index) constructed from a poverty line (Medeiros); 0<k<1
the inequality of the whole distribution, not a focus on the upper tail

output_key_fields: index (richness_index): the affluence index; hc and cha lie in [0,1] as ratios, fgt is non-negative but NOT bounded above, and med is absolute, in income units
index_type (richness_index): hc, cha, fgt or med (a closed enum, default hc)
affluence_line (richness_index): rho = k times the weighted median — the UPPER threshold that was used; median_income is the median itself
count_rich / share_rich / k / n (richness_index): the number of units above rho, the weighted share of the rich, the value of k, and the sample size
income_share (income_share_top): the income share of those above the p-quantile, in [0,1]; threshold_quantile is that quantile; top_fraction is 1-p (p=0.9 gives the top 10%); plus count_top and n
affluence_line: the Medeiros affluence line; median_multiple = rho/median, above 1; median_income; poverty_gap; k; n
interpretation_traps: THRESHOLD DIRECTION (critical): the affluence line is an UPPER threshold. richness_index requires k>1, so that rho = k times the median sits above the median; k<=1 puts the line at or below the median and makes 'everyone rich' (live: k=0.5 gives a headcount of 0.9, k=1 gives 0.4). A gate blocks it
the OPPOSITE meaning of k: in affluence_line, k defines a POVERTY line BELOW the median, so 0<k<1; it mirrors richness_index — do not confuse the two
fgt is NOT bounded by 1 (it is convex, gaps^alpha; live alpha=3 → 1.27, a large alpha + a heavy tail → an overflow to Inf that the post-gate blocks); only hc/cha ∈ [0,1]; med is absolute
alpha>1 for fgt, and beta>0 for cha: the raw routine does NOT check the domain (live, alpha=0.5 was computed silently); the wrapper enforces it, and only for the relevant index
positive income (x>0): the raw routine does NOT error on negative or zero values — live, a negative input still returned a number; the wrapper blocks them, since the cha index divides by x

weights: the same length as x, with no recycling, strictly positive and with no gaps; leaving them unset gives equal weights. The weighted median and quantile use the SAME routine the index calls internally, so the reported rho and quantile are identical to the internal threshold

income_share_top: p is the QUANTILE threshold in (0,1), and the index measures the richest 1-p tail (p=0.9 gives the top 10%); it is not 'the top p%'; the extremes degenerate — p towards 0 gives about 1, p towards 1 gives 0 — and are blocked

affluence_line (Medeiros): the line MUST lie ABOVE the median (median_multiple>1, a hard post-gate); a degenerate line at or below the median is blocked, since it would make everyone 'rich'; an x with zero dispersion, fewer than two distinct values, trips a pre-gate; and a matrix with more than one column trips another — vectors, or a single column, only
sources: Peichl, Schaefer, Scheicher 2008 IZA Discussion Paper 3790 (measuring richness — affluence indices, axioms T1/T2)
Chakravarty 1983 Mathematical Social Sciences 6:307-313 (the concave index, the T1 mirror)
Foster, Greer, Thorbecke 1984 Econometrica 52:761-766 (the FGT decomposable family, the convex T2 mirror)
Medeiros 2006 Social Indicators Research 78:1-18 (an affluence line constructed from the poverty line)
Brzezinski 2010 Social Indicators Research 99:285-299 (income affluence in Poland; the richness headcount & top income share)

cards.when: headcount, gap and severity of poverty from survey data, with standard errors that respect the survey design
cards.when_not: the data are not a probability sample; the poverty line is not defined

alternatives.criterion: headcount, gap and severity in one family
a relative line at a share of median income
combines incidence, depth and inequality among the poor

output_key_fields: fgt: the measures at alpha 0, 1 and 2
poverty_line: the line used and how it was set
se, conf_int: design-based inference
decomposition: contributions by subgroup
interpretation_traps: THE HEADCOUNT IS INSENSITIVE TO HOW POOR THE POOR ARE: a transfer to the least poor person can reduce it while worsening the gap, which is why the FGT family exists
a relative poverty line moves with the median, so poverty can fall in a recession as the median falls -- that is arithmetic, not improvement
naive standard errors ignoring the survey design understate uncertainty substantially in clustered samples
sources: Foster, Greer & Thorbecke 1984 (Econometrica 52:761-766)
Sen 1976 (Econometrica 44:219)
svy

cards.when: the top of the income or wealth distribution is thin in surveys and heavy in reality, and a parametric tail is needed to say anything about it
cards.when_not: the top is well measured; there are too few top observations for a tail index to be estimated

alternatives.criterion: a single tail index
a semi-parametric index without fixing the threshold model
you want a full tail distribution, not one parameter

output_key_fields: alpha: the Pareto tail index; lower means heavier
threshold: where the tail begins
top_shares: shares of the top percentiles
goodness_of_fit: whether the Pareto assumption holds above the threshold
interpretation_traps: THE HILL ESTIMATOR IS ACUTELY SENSITIVE TO THE THRESHOLD, and the Hill plot is usually unstable enough that any index in a wide range can be justified
survey data systematically under-cover the top, so a tail fitted to survey data understates concentration regardless of the estimator
an index below 2 means infinite variance and below 1 an infinite mean, which invalidates many downstream statistics
sources: Clauset, Shalizi & Newman 2009 (SIAM Review 51:661-703)
Blanchet, Fournier & Piketty 2022 (Review of Income and Wealth 68:357)
powerlaw

cards.when: measuring how unevenly groups are distributed across areas, schools or firms
cards.when_not: there are only two areas, where the indices are degenerate; the group definition is not stable across units

alternatives.criterion: two groups, the standard measure
the experience of a group rather than evenness
more than two groups

output_key_fields: index: the requested segregation measure
decomposition: between and within larger areas
se: inference by simulation or bootstrap
n_units: the number of areas, which drives the bias
interpretation_traps: SEGREGATION INDICES ARE BIASED UPWARD WHEN UNITS ARE SMALL, because random allocation produces uneven counts -- the bias correction is not optional with small areas
the dissimilarity index measures evenness only; two cities with identical indices can differ completely in isolation and exposure
changing the areal unit changes the index, which is the modifiable areal unit problem in its purest form
sources: Duncan & Duncan 1955 (American Sociological Review 20:210-217)
Massey & Denton 1988 (Social Forces 67:281)
Reardon & Firebaugh 2002 (Sociological Methodology 32:33)
segregation

cards.when: splitting national inequality into what happens between regions and what happens within them
cards.when_not: there is no spatial dimension; the regional classification is unstable over the period

alternatives.criterion: exactly additive between and within
you want a Gini that accounts for neighbourhood
the Gini does not decompose cleanly and leaves a residual

output_key_fields: between, within: the two components
shares: each component's share of the total
by_region: within-region inequality per region
spatial_component: the neighbour-based part, where the spatial Gini is used
interpretation_traps: THE GINI DOES NOT DECOMPOSE ADDITIVELY when subgroup distributions overlap -- it leaves a residual overlap term, which is why the Theil index is used for decomposition
the between-share depends entirely on the regional classification; finer regions mechanically raise it
population-weighted and unweighted regional inequality answer different questions
sources: Shorrocks 1980 (Econometrica 48:613-625)
Rey & Smith 2013 (Letters in Spatial and Resource Sciences 6:189)
inequality

cards.when: measuring how much economic position persists between generations or over time, which inequality snapshots cannot show
cards.when_not: only one period or generation is observed; the linkage between generations is not reliable

alternatives.criterion: robust, scale free, the modern standard
the classic log-log measure, sensitive to lifecycle bias
you want the full mobility pattern

output_key_fields: rank_rank: the slope of child rank on parent rank
ige: the intergenerational elasticity
transition_matrix: quintile or decile mobility
upward_mobility: the expected rank of children from the bottom
interpretation_traps: THE INTERGENERATIONAL ELASTICITY IS SENSITIVE TO THE AGE AT WHICH INCOME IS MEASURED (lifecycle bias) and to changing inequality between generations; the rank-rank slope is robust to both, which is why it replaced it
single-year income is a noisy proxy for permanent income and attenuates every mobility measure
transition matrices with many cells and few observations produce zero probabilities that are artefacts of sample size
sources: Chetty, Hendren, Kline & Saez 2014 (Quarterly Journal of Economics 129:1553-1623)
Solon 1992 (American Economic Review 82:393)
giddy

cards.when: inequality measures cannot distinguish a spread-out distribution from one splitting into clusters, and polarisation is about the clustering
cards.when_not: the distribution is plainly unimodal and no clustering is suspected

alternatives.criterion: bipolarisation around the median
general polarisation with an identification-alienation structure
the classic bipolarisation measure

output_key_fields: polarisation: the requested index
identification, alienation: the two components of the Esteban-Ray form
median_split: shares above and below the median
comparison: the Gini, for contrast
interpretation_traps: POLARISATION AND INEQUALITY CAN MOVE IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS: a transfer from a rich person to a middle-income person lowers the Gini and can raise bipolarisation
the Esteban-Ray index depends on a sensitivity parameter with no natural value; results must be reported across a range
polarisation measures require grouping or smoothing, and the grouping choice drives the identification component
sources: Esteban & Ray 1994 (Econometrica 62:819-851)
Wolfson 1994 (American Economic Review 84:353)
Foster & Wolfson 2010 (Journal of Economic Inequality 8:247)
ineqpy

cards.method: Equivalence scales and household-to-individual welfare aggregation
cards.when: household income must be adjusted for size and composition before it can be compared, and the scale chosen changes every distributional conclusion
cards.when_not: the unit of analysis is the household itself; the composition data needed for the scale are missing

alternatives.criterion: the European standard
simple, widely used in OECD comparisons
no economies of scale assumed

output_key_fields: equivalised: equivalised income per person
scale_values: the equivalence factor per household
sensitivity: how inequality and poverty move across scales
elasticity: the implied economies-of-scale elasticity
interpretation_traps: THE SCALE CHOICE MATERIALLY CHANGES MEASURED INEQUALITY AND POVERTY, and it changes them differently for households of different types -- reporting a sensitivity range is the honest practice
equivalised income is assigned to every household member, which assumes equal sharing within the household -- an assumption with no support in the data
comparisons across countries using different national scales are not comparable
sources: Buhmann, Rainwater, Schmaus & Smeeding 1988 (Review of Income and Wealth 34:115-142)
OECD 2013, Framework for Statistics on the Distribution of Household Income
